title: How the king moves
outcomes: Taps the squares a king can step to, never onto an attacked square or next to the enemy king
Says in a sentence why the king avoids attacked squares

steps.text: The **king** moves one square in any direction, straight or diagonal. That is eight squares in the open, fewer at an edge. Losing the king loses the game, so it moves with care. It can also capture an enemy piece, if that piece is not protected. Castling is a special extra move that comes later.

steps.caption: From e4 the king can reach any of the eight squares around it.

line.say: A diagonal step is still only one square.
Black's king takes a step of its own.

steps.text: A king may never step onto a square the enemy **attacks** (a square where an enemy piece could capture it), and never next to the enemy king. If the king stepped there, the enemy could capture it next move, and the king may never be captured, so that move is simply not allowed. The full rule comes with check; for now, cross those squares out.

steps.caption: The black rook on h3 attacks every square along the third rank (the arrow). The five marked squares are the ones the king may use.

line.say: Rank four is not on the rook's line, so d4 is safe.

steps.caption: The black king on e6 attacks d5, e5 and f5, just as the white king attacks the squares around e4. So the white king may not go to those three.

line.say: One empty square between the kings is allowed.

steps.text: The king captures like it moves: one square. But it may only take a piece that is **not protected**. If a friend of that piece could take back on the square, the king would be captured, so the capture is not allowed.

steps.prompt: Say it back. Explain to a friend why the white king cannot go to e3 in the rook position, and which other squares are off limits. Then read the model answer.

steps.text: **Model answer.** The king steps one square any way, but never onto a square an enemy piece attacks (the rook covers the whole third rank) and never next to the enemy king. If it stepped there it could be captured, and the king may never be captured. Before a king move, check the enemy pieces' lines and the squares around the enemy king.
